Case Vignette: Dr. M.

Dr. M. is a 63-year-old married North American physician who presents for an initial consultation at the urging of his wife. He is a tall, fit man with a measured, deliberate way of speaking, though his hands tremble slightly as he folds them in his lap. He has been a family practice doctor for nearly forty years, and describes himself as someone who has "seen it all." He begins his story by saying, "I used to think I was unshakable."

The trauma occurred three years ago, during a medical mission trip to a conflict zone. Dr. M. was working in a field hospital when a coordinated bombing and shooting attack struck the compound. He describes the first ten minutes in vivid, sensory detail: the ground shaking, the sound of automatic gunfire, the smell of diesel and blood. He was in the triage tent when a young woman was carried in, her leg nearly severed. He remembers the weight of the tourniquet in his hands, the way her eyes rolled back, and then the second explosion that blew out the tent walls. He does not remember finishing the surgery. He does not remember how he got to the evacuation helicopter. He only remembers waking up in a military hospital two days later, with a broken collarbone and a concussion.

For the first year after returning home, Dr. M. did not speak about the attack. He told his wife he was "fine," that he was "processing it in his own way." He returned to work within three weeks. But his wife noticed changes. He stopped watching the evening news. He became irritable during family dinners, snapping at his adult children for small things. He began drinking two glasses of whiskey every night to "unwind," something he had never done before.

In the past year, the symptoms have worsened. Dr. M. now avoids the hospital break room because it reminds him of the triage tent. He has stopped performing minor surgical procedures in his office because the sight of blood makes his heart race and his vision blur. He experiences intrusive images of the young woman's face-not every day, but several times a week, often when he is trying to fall asleep. He feels a tightness in his chest and a sense of dread that he cannot explain. He has become hypervigilant in public spaces, scanning crowds for threats, and he no longer attends his weekly church choir practice because the small, crowded room feels "too dangerous."

His wife reports that he has become emotionally distant. He no longer initiates physical affection, and he has withdrawn from their long-standing Sunday morning coffee ritual. He tells me he feels "numb" and "disconnected," as if he is watching his own life from a distance. He has trouble concentrating on patient charts and has made two minor medication errors in the last six months, which he finds deeply shameful. He has not told his colleagues about the trauma.

At the end of our first session, Dr. M. looks at his hands and says, quietly, "I used to be the one who fixed things. Now I can't even fix myself." He does not meet my eyes. He is a man who has spent his life caring for others, and now, for the first time, he is allowing himself to be seen as someone who needs care.
